unit.title: Scoring and Rotation
unit.summary: Side-out and rally scoring rules, the three-number score call, server rotation, the 0-0-2 start, and why court position matters.

lessons.title: Only the server scores
lessons.objective: Explain side-out scoring and why the serving advantage matters.

payload.prompt: In side-out scoring, what happens when the receiving team wins a rally?

options.text: They gain the serve without scoring (side-out)

explanation.correct: Side-out means the receiving team wins the serve, but no one scores a point. Only the serving side can score.
explanation.incorrect: In side-out scoring, only the server scores points. The receiving team gets the serve if they win, but with zero points.
explanation.sayThisLine: Side-out: you win the serve but don't score until you serve.

payload.prompt: Complete the side-out rule.
payload.template: Only the {{scorer}} scores points in side-out scoring; the other team must {{action}} to start scoring.

explanation.correct: The serving team scores; the receiving team must win the serve to start accumulating points of their own.
explanation.incorrect: Side-out scoring reserves scoring for the serving team. The receiving team gains the serve (side-out) with no points.
explanation.sayThisLine: Server scores; you get the serve to start scoring.

payload.prompt: Your team is receiving. You win the rally. Do you score?

situation.narrative: It's 3-2 in side-out scoring, your team is receiving. You hit a clean winner.

options.label: You gain the serve but don't score
options.consequence: You become the serving team with the score still 3-2. Now you can start scoring points.
considerations: Side-out scoring only lets the server score
Winning the rally as receiver = side-out (gain serve)
Next point you play will be your first chance to score

options.label: You score one point
options.consequence: Incorrect. The receiving team never scores in side-out; you gain the serve to start scoring.
considerations: This is the core rule of side-out
You must serve to accumulate points
Side-out is 'serve to score'

payload.expertNote: Side-out scoring makes the serve extremely valuable. The serving team can run up a lead; the receiving team must win the serve first to score.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: We won that rally but didn't score? That doesn't make sense.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: You're receiving, so you get the serve (side-out) but no points yet. You score when you serve.
That's just the rule; nobody knows why.

payload.translation: Side-out scoring means the serving side has the scoring advantage. You must win the serve before you can start scoring.

followUps.line: You got the serve (side-out). Now you score on your serves until they win.
followUps.why: Explains the rule and its effect clearly.

followUps.line: Side-out scoring: only the server scores. You won the serve, which is huge.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Side-out is the foundation of pickleball scoring strategy. Winning the serve is as important as scoring points.

payload.prompt: Receiving team wins the rally 5-6. Score is now what?

scene.alt: Score scenario: serving 5-6, receiving wins the rally.

explanation.correct: Correct. Receiving won, so they get the serve (side-out), but the score stays 5-6 in side-out. No points are awarded.
explanation.incorrect: Side-out scoring doesn't award points to the receiving team. They get the serve, but the score stays the same.
explanation.sayThisLine: Side-out, they gain the serve at 5-6.

lessons.title: The three-number call
lessons.objective: Read and call a doubles score as three numbers.

payload.prompt: What do the three numbers in '4-3-2' represent?

options.text: Server one score, server two score, receiver score
Serving team score, receiving team score, server number

explanation.correct: In doubles, the call is always serving team score, receiving team score, server number (1 or 2).
explanation.incorrect: The three numbers are: serving team, receiving team, then which server (server one or server two) is currently serving.
explanation.sayThisLine: Three numbers: server score, receiver score, server one or two.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Serving team is at 6, receiving is at 5, and server one is serving.
It's the first game, no idea what the other numbers mean.

payload.translation: The three-number call tells you who's ahead and which server is up. It's the official way to call score in doubles.

followUps.line: The first number is the server's score, second is the receiver's, third is server one or two.
followUps.why: Breaks it down into memorable parts.

followUps.line: 6-5-1 means server is ahead 6 to 5, and it's the first server's turn.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The three-number call is standard and becomes automatic once you use it a few times.

payload.prompt: Match each part of a three-number score call to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Which server is currently serving (1 or 2)

explanation.summary: The three-number call in doubles is always: serving team score, receiving team score, server number. This format is standard everywhere.
explanation.sayThisLine: Server score, receiver score, server one or two.

payload.prompt: Complete the three-number rule.
payload.template: A doubles score is called {{num1}}, {{num2}}, {{num3}}, where the last number is always 1 or 2.

explanation.correct: The three-number call is universal in doubles: server, receiver, then server one or two.
explanation.incorrect: Always remember the order: serving team first, receiving second, server number third (1 or 2).
explanation.sayThisLine: Three numbers: server, receiver, and which server's turn.

payload.prompt: You need to call the score. What is it?

situation.narrative: You're keeping score. The serving team has 7 points, the receiving team has 4, and it's the second server's turn.

options.label: Call it 7-4-2
options.consequence: Correct. Seven (server), four (receiver), two (server two is serving). This is the proper three-number call.
considerations: 7 for the serving team
4 for the receiving team
2 because server two is up

options.label: Call it 4-7-2
options.consequence: Incorrect order. The serving team score always comes first in the three-number call.
considerations: Server score first, receiver score second
Confusing scores makes play confusing
Get the order right for clarity

payload.expertNote: The three-number call is always consistent: serving team, receiving team, server number. Learn the order and you'll call it right every time.

lessons.title: Server one, server two, side out
lessons.objective: Follow the serve through both partners and know when the serve moves to the other team.

payload.prompt: Put the serve sequence in order (how it moves through both servers).

items.text: Server one serves and wins the rally
items.why: The first partner gets the serve at the start.

items.text: Server one serves and loses the rally
items.why: First server is out; the serve moves to server two.

items.text: Server two now serves and wins the rally
items.why: The second partner gets a chance to serve.

items.text: Server two serves and loses the rally
items.why: Both servers are out; it's a side-out.
The serve goes to the other team because both partners lost.

explanation.correct: Server one goes first, then server two, then side-out. Once both servers lose, the entire serve moves to the receiving team.
explanation.incorrect: Each partner gets a turn to serve (unless they win). After both lose, the whole serve goes to the other team.
explanation.sayThisLine: Server one, then server two, then side-out to the other team.

payload.prompt: Server one loses a rally. The serve moves to...?

scene.alt: Serve scenario: server one just lost the rally.

explanation.correct: Server one is out, so the serve goes to server two on the same team. Only after server two loses does it go to the other team (side-out).
explanation.incorrect: Each team gets two servers (both partners). Server one losing means server two gets a turn; side-out happens only after both lose.
explanation.sayThisLine: Server one out, server two gets the serve.

payload.prompt: Server two just lost. The serve moves to...?

scene.alt: Serve scenario: server two just lost the rally, completing the pair's turn.

explanation.correct: Both servers on the serving team have lost; it's a side-out. The receiving team now serves.
explanation.incorrect: When both partners lose, the serve goes to the receiving team. You don't start over with server one.
explanation.sayThisLine: Side-out, they get the serve.

payload.prompt: Complete the server rotation rule.
payload.template: The serve goes to {{first}}, then {{second}}, then a {{third}} to the other team if both lose.

explanation.correct: Both partners on the serving team get a turn. After both lose a rally, side-out sends the serve to the other team.
explanation.incorrect: Each serving team has two servers. Only after both serve and lose does the other team get the serve.
explanation.sayThisLine: Server one, server two, then side-out.

payload.prompt: Server one wins the rally. Where does the serve go next?

situation.narrative: Server one just won a rally. The score is now 7-2 (server's team is winning).

facts.label: Outcome
facts.value: They can run up their score

options.label: Server one keeps serving
options.consequence: Correct. When you win, you serve again. Server one can keep serving until they lose.
considerations: Winning the rally = you keep the serve
Server one plays until they lose
Then server two gets their chance

options.label: Serve goes to server two
options.consequence: Incorrect. You only move to the other partner after losing, not after winning.
considerations: Winning keeps you serving
Losing moves to the other server
Side-out happens after both lose

payload.expertNote: The serving team can run long scoring streaks. As long as they keep winning, the serve stays with them (server one, then server two if needed).

lessons.title: The 0-0-2 start
lessons.objective: Know why the first serving team starts with only one server.

payload.prompt: At the start of a match, why does the first serving team start at 0-0-2?

options.text: To give the receiving team a fair chance; serving is an advantage

explanation.correct: The first server only gets one turn (0-0-2 means server two is marked, but server one serves alone at the start). This evens out the advantage of serving first.
explanation.incorrect: Serving is a scoring advantage in side-out scoring, so the first serving team starts with only one server as a handicap. It's fair, not random.
explanation.sayThisLine: 0-0-2 means the first team serves once, then it's the other team's turn.

payload.prompt: The match just started at 0-0-2. Server one wins the rally. What's next?

situation.narrative: Score is 0-0-2, the first team just won. They're on the board and in control.

facts.label: Fair advantage
facts.value: First server gets one shot, then other team serves

options.label: Server one serves again
options.consequence: Correct. Winning the rally means the serve stays. Server one keeps serving until they lose.
considerations: Winning keeps you serving
0-0-2 is just the starting mark
Losing ends server one's turn, side-out happens next

options.label: Other team gets the serve immediately
options.consequence: Incorrect. 0-0-2 is just the starting score. Server one can keep serving if winning.
considerations: 0-0-2 means server one serves alone at the start
But they still follow normal serve rules (win = keep, lose = other team)

payload.expertNote: 0-0-2 is only the starting format. After the first serve, the game plays normally: winners keep serving, losers move to the next server or side-out.

payload.prompt: Complete the 0-0-2 rule.
payload.template: At the start of a match, the score is 0-0-2, meaning only {{server}} on the first serving team gets to serve initially.

explanation.correct: 0-0-2 is the starting score: serving team is 0, receiving is 0, and the mark '2' means server two is waiting (server one goes first and alone).
explanation.incorrect: At the start, only server one serves. The '2' marks server two as next in line. This balances the serving advantage.
explanation.sayThisLine: 0-0-2 is the start: server one only, then everyone else follows normal rules.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: Why does the first team only get one server at 0-0-2?

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Serving is an advantage in side-out, so the first team gets only one server to make it fair.
I don't know, that's just the rule.
It's a penalty for being first.
So the other team can catch up faster.

payload.translation: In side-out scoring, only the server scores. So the first serving team has a big advantage. The 0-0-2 rule handicaps them by giving them only one server at the start, evening things out.

followUps.line: Serving is huge in side-out scoring. Getting only one server at the start is a trade-off for that advantage.
After server one is out, the other team serves. It keeps the match fair.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The 0-0-2 rule is not a penalty; it's a fairness adjustment for the server's scoring advantage.

payload.prompt: Match just started. Score is 0-0-2. Server one loses the first rally. What now?

scene.alt: Starting scenario: first team has 0-0-2, server one just lost.

explanation.correct: At 0-0-2, there is no server two. The first team only gets server one. When server one loses, it goes straight to side-out (the other team).
explanation.incorrect: 0-0-2 means no server two at the start. Server one serves and loses, so it's a side-out immediately.
explanation.sayThisLine: Side-out, the other team serves.

lessons.title: Even right, odd left
lessons.objective: Pick the service side based on the serving team's score.

payload.prompt: Score is 5-3-1. Server one is serving. Which side?

diagram.alt: Top-down pickleball court showing left and right service sides.

explanation.correct: Server's score is 5 (odd), so server one stands on the left side. Odd = left.
explanation.incorrect: When the server's score is odd (5), the server stands on the left. When even (4, 6, etc.), the server stands on the right.
explanation.sayThisLine: Odd score means left side, even means right.

payload.prompt: Score is 6-4-2. Which side does server two serve from?

explanation.correct: Server's score is 6 (even), so server two serves from the right side. Even = right.
explanation.incorrect: The serving team's score is 6 (even), which means right side. Left is for odd scores.
explanation.sayThisLine: Even score means right side; odd means left.

payload.prompt: Score is 3-2-1. Where does server one start?

explanation.correct: Score is 3 (odd), so server one stands on the left side. Odd scores = left side; even scores = right side.
explanation.incorrect: For serving position, use the server's team score: 3 is odd, which means left side.
explanation.sayThisLine: Odd score means left side; even means right.

payload.prompt: Complete the serving position rule.
payload.template: If the serving team's score is {{even}}, the server stands on the right; if {{odd}}, on the left.

explanation.correct: Even score = right side. Odd score = left side. This applies every single serve.
explanation.incorrect: The rule is consistent: even right, odd left. It determines which service box the server serves from on each rally.
explanation.sayThisLine: Even right, odd left. That's how you know where to stand.

payload.prompt: Score is 2-1-1. Where does server one serve from?

situation.narrative: The serving team has 2 points. Server one is up. Where on the baseline does server one stand?

options.label: Right side (server's right)
options.consequence: Correct. Score is 2 (even), so server one stands on the right side and serves from the right service box.
considerations: 2 points is even
Even score = right side
Server stands behind the right baseline

options.label: Left side (server's left)
options.consequence: Incorrect. 2 is even, not odd. Even = right side.
considerations: Left side is for odd scores (1, 3, 5, etc.)
2 is even, so right side
Remember: even right, odd left

payload.expertNote: The even-odd rule is automatic once you practice it. It ensures both servers start each game from the same side and keeps rotation consistent.

payload.prompt: Estimate the winning score if a game goes to 11-10.

explanation.correct: If it's 11-10, the leader must win by 2. They need 13 to win (11+2). It's 13-11 final.
explanation.incorrect: Win by 2 means a 2-point margin. From 11-10, you need 13-11 to finish.
explanation.sayThisLine: Eleven to start, but you must win by two.

payload.prompt: What's the minimum winning score in a standard pickleball game?

explanation.correct: 11 is the target, win by 2. So 11-9 ends it, but 11-10 requires 13-11.
explanation.incorrect: Pickleball games are to 11 (not 21 like some other sports), and you must win by a 2-point margin.
explanation.sayThisLine: Games to 11, win by two minimum points.

payload.prompt: What is a standard pickleball match format?

explanation.correct: A match is best of three: first team to win two games wins the match.
explanation.incorrect: Pickleball matches are typically best of three games. Win two games and you win the match.
explanation.sayThisLine: Matches are best of three games.

payload.prompt: Complete the game and match rules.
payload.template: A game is played to {{goal}} and won by {{margin}}; a match is {{format}} games.

explanation.correct: Games to 11, win by 2. Matches are best of three (first to 2 games wins the match).
explanation.incorrect: Standard pickleball: game to 11 (win by 2), match is best of three games.
explanation.sayThisLine: Eleven, win by two; match is best of three games.

payload.prompt: It's a match. Your team won game one 11-8. Game two is at 10-9 in your favor. What's at stake?

situation.narrative: Match is best of three. You're up 1-0 in games. Game two is close.

facts.label: Stakes
facts.value: One more game win ends the match

options.label: If you win this game, you win the match
options.consequence: Correct. You're 1-0 in games; winning this game makes it 2-0 and ends the match.
considerations: Matches are best of three games
First to 2 games wins
This is match point (game-point)

options.label: If you win, it goes 1-1 and requires a tiebreak
options.consequence: Incorrect. You're already 1-0 up. One more win and it's 2-0, match over.
considerations: You already won game one
Best of three means first to 2 wins the match
This is your match point

payload.expertNote: In a best-of-three match, being up 1-0 with a lead in game two is critical: one win ends it, one loss ties it 1-1 and forces a third game.

lessons.title: Rally scoring
lessons.objective: Explain rally scoring and where it is used.

payload.prompt: In rally scoring, what happens every rally?

options.text: Only the server scores if they win
Whoever wins the rally scores a point
No one scores until a team reaches 5

explanation.correct: Rally scoring means every rally = one point. Whoever wins the rally scores, regardless of who's serving.
explanation.incorrect: This is opposite to side-out scoring. Rally scoring gives a point to the rally winner, always.
explanation.sayThisLine: Rally scoring: every rally, somebody scores.

payload.prompt: Match the scoring types to their rule.

pairs.definition: Only the serving team scores points; receiving team must win the serve first.
Every rally awards a point to the winner, regardless of who is serving.
In side-out scoring, the server has an edge because they accumulate points while serving.

explanation.summary: Side-out is traditional; rally scoring is newer and optional. Both are legal, but used in different contexts.
explanation.sayThisLine: Side-out: server only. Rally: everybody scores on every rally.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: We played rally scoring tonight. It's so different.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Yeah, every rally somebody scores. Do you prefer it over side-out?
I don't know what that means.

payload.translation: Rally scoring is a newer option where every rally scores a point for the winner. It changes strategy compared to side-out.

followUps.line: The pro tours use rally scoring sometimes. Did it change how you played?
followUps.why: Shows you know the context and invites her reflection.

followUps.line: Every rally counts instead of just serves. Does that speed things up?
followUps.why: A thoughtful question about the effect.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Rally scoring is debated in the community. Some love it, some prefer side-out. Listen to her thoughts without picking a side.

payload.prompt: Complete the rally scoring rule.
payload.template: In rally scoring, {{who}} wins the rally {{when}} scores a point, and games are usually to {{points}}.

explanation.correct: Rally scoring: every rally scores. Games may be to 11, 15, or 21 depending on the format.
explanation.incorrect: Rally scoring is always: rally winner scores. The target score may vary by format.
explanation.sayThisLine: Rally scoring, every rally counts.

payload.prompt: You're receiving and you win the rally. Under rally scoring, do you score?

situation.narrative: Rally scoring is in effect. You're on the receiving team and you win the rally.

options.label: Yes, you score a point
options.consequence: Correct. In rally scoring, the rally winner scores, no matter who's serving. You won, so you score.
considerations: Rally scoring = every rally counts
You don't have to serve to score
Different from side-out

options.label: No, you only gain the serve
options.consequence: Incorrect. That's side-out scoring. Rally scoring gives you a point for winning the rally.
considerations: Rally scoring means everybody can score
You don't need to serve to score
This is the key difference from side-out

payload.expertNote: Rally scoring flattens the scoring advantage of serving and is used in some pro events and recreational formats. It's a game-changer strategically.

lessons.title: Keep the score, keep the peace
lessons.objective: Track a full game and settle a score dispute.

payload.prompt: There's a score dispute: one team says 7-5-1, the other says 5-7-1. How do you resolve it?

situation.narrative: Two partners disagree on the score. One team thinks they're ahead 7-5, the other says 5-7.

options.label: Recount the rally points calmly; when in doubt, go to the lower score
options.consequence: Smart. Recount if you can, or default to the lower score (benefit of the doubt = ball is in). This keeps the game fair and friendly.
considerations: Honest recount is best
Benefit of doubt favors the other team on disputes
Peace is as important as accuracy

options.label: Demand the other team prove their score; if not, call them liars
options.consequence: Escalation. Accusations end games and friendships. Disputes are normal in recreational play. Resolve calmly.
considerations: Conflict turns people away from the game
Honest dispute resolution protects the community
Benefit of the doubt is standard etiquette

payload.expertNote: Recreational pickleball depends on honesty and grace under ambiguity. Defaulting to the lower score on disputes is built into the honor code.

payload.prompt: It's match point. Team A leads 10-8. Server A1 wins the rally. What's the new score?

scene.alt: Match-point scenario: 10-8, server one won the rally.

explanation.correct: Server A1 won, so the score goes to 11-8 and the server number stays 1 (server one stays serving when they win).
explanation.incorrect: When server one wins, server one keeps serving. The server number doesn't change.
explanation.sayThisLine: Winners keep serving, same server number.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: Wait, what's the score? I lost track after all those fast rallies.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Let me think... serving team is at 6, receiving at 4, and it's server two. So 6-4-2.

payload.translation: If you're keeping score, the three-number call is your responsibility: serving team, receiving team, server number. It keeps everyone on the same page.

followUps.line: 6-4-2: serving team has 6, receiving has 4, and server two is up. Write it down next time.
followUps.why: Specific and helpful, plus a tip for the future.

followUps.line: Whoever is keeping score, just call it out loud each rally. Keeps everyone aligned.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Being the score-keeper is important. It's not hard once you practice the three-number call.
